docs.title: How DevPulse is built
docs.lede: Technical choices and why they were made, security, automation, deployment, and how an AI coding agent is used responsibly. A public summary; the repository holds the full details.

blocks.text: DevPulse analyses public GitHub repositories. Its first analysis, the branch report, is available as a web application and as a command-line tool. The project is also a showcase of how a small product is designed, secured, tested, automated and run in production by one engineer working with an AI coding agent.

Every technical decision is recorded as an [Architecture Decision Record](https://github.com/BrahimNJ/DevPulse/tree/main/docs/decisions) with the alternatives that were rejected. This page summarises them; the records hold the details.

The code is layered: a **domain** layer computes the report from plain data and an injected clock, an **infrastructure** layer talks to GitHub, and the **interfaces** (web API, React application, CLI) depend on both, never the reverse. This is why the business rules are tested without any network.

head: Choice
Why
rows: TypeScript, strict
Type errors are caught before running; strict mode removes whole classes of bugs.
Node.js 24 running TypeScript directly
No compile step for the server: what is tested is what runs.
Node standard library first
HTTP server, tests, compression, crypto: fewer dependencies, smaller attack surface.
React and Vite
A maintainable interface with a fast build; plain CSS on a dark theme, animated with Motion.
GitHub GraphQL API
100 branches with their last commit and divergence per request, instead of one REST call per branch.
Docker, distroless image
One reproducible artefact; no shell or package manager in production.
Google Cloud Run
Containers that scale to zero: no server to patch and no cost when idle.
Terraform
The whole cloud project is code, reviewed in pull requests and reproducible.
GitHub Actions
Checks, builds and deployments live next to the code, pinned and auditable.

items: **No secret in the browser or the repository.** The GitHub token lives in Secret Manager and is only readable by the server's own identity.
**No long-lived cloud key.** Deployments exchange a short-lived GitHub identity token for Google credentials (Workload Identity Federation), and only the main branch of this repository is accepted.
**Least privilege.** Each service account can do one job: run the server, deploy it, or stop billing. None can do the others' work.
**Strict HTTP headers.** Content Security Policy without inline code, HSTS, no framing, no MIME sniffing, no referrer, no CORS.
**Host validation.** The server only answers its own names, which blocks DNS rebinding attacks.
**Hardened container.** Non-root user, read-only files, no shell, base images pinned by digest and scanned for vulnerabilities on every change.
**Supply chain.** Every CI action is pinned to a commit, every image is signed with a provenance attestation and a bill of materials, and secret scanning runs on every pull request.

**Privacy.** Client addresses are never logged or stored; the daily allowance keeps only a salted hash and the repositories analysed, which expire after 24 hours and are deleted shortly after. Usage statistics for the maintainer record each analysis under the same pseudonymous hash, with the report, the repository, the outcome, its duration, whether the cache answered, a coarse device class (mobile, desktop or bot) and the browser's first language; they are deleted after 30 days.

blocks.text: All visitors share one GitHub token, so the service protects it in layers, from the cheapest to the strictest:

items: A 10-minute cache: a popular repository costs one call, however many people open it.
Concurrent requests for the same repository share a single call.
A per-minute rate limit per client.
Three analyses per visitor per 24 hours, stored server-side, so refreshing the page or opening a private window does not reset them. Re-opening a repository is free.
A reserve: below a safety margin of GitHub quota, new reports are refused.
A timeout, so a huge repository cannot hold the server.

blocks.text: Every change, however small, follows the same path:

items: An issue describes the problem.
A branch named after the type of change is created from main.
Commits follow Conventional Commits and explain why, one concern each.
A pull request uses a template and is reviewed; main is never pushed to directly.
release-please reads the commits, writes the changelog and proposes the next version.

blocks.text: Git hooks format and lint staged files and check commit messages before anything leaves the machine; CI runs the same checks again on GitHub.

head: When
What runs
rows: On every pull request
Formatting, linting, types, tests, commit messages, dependency audit, secret scan, container build and vulnerability scan, infrastructure validation.
On every merge to main
The image is built once, signed, pushed, deployed to a private staging service and smoke tested.
On every release
After the maintainer approves, the same image is deployed to production without traffic, checked, then switched on; a failed check switches back automatically.
Every week
Dependabot proposes updates of dependencies, actions and base images.

blocks.text: Building once and promoting the same image means production runs exactly what was tested in staging.

The service runs on Cloud Run in Europe, scaled to zero when nobody uses it, sized to stay within Google Cloud's free tier. Infrastructure is described in Terraform: services, registry, identities, secrets, database, monitoring and budget.

items: An uptime check alerts the maintainer by email if production stops answering.
Logs are structured, so they can be searched by status, latency and cache use.

A monthly budget emails at 10%, 50% and 100%, and a small function detaches billing from the project when the budget is reached: a hard spending stop, verified end to end in production without being triggered.

blocks.text: The project is built with Claude Code, an AI coding agent, configured in the repository so that its behaviour is shared, reviewed and enforced rather than improvised.

head: Mechanism
Role
rows: Project instructions
Short rules loaded in every session: scope discipline, workflow, hard limits such as never committing secrets.
Skills
Repeatable workflows as commands: create an issue, start work, check, commit, open a pull request.
Subagents
Specialists with their own context and minimal tools: a code reviewer, an explorer, a writer of decision records.
Hooks
Checks the harness enforces itself: protected files cannot be edited, edited files are formatted.
Human in the loop
Plans are approved before edits, and cloud changes and production releases are applied by the maintainer.

blocks.text: Every pull request is reviewed by a review subagent before it is opened; its findings and the fixes they led to are recorded in each pull request.

The Delivery tab reads the last 90 days of a repository: the 100 most recently merged pull requests with their first reviews, the releases, and search counts. It costs one GitHub API point and is cached for 10 minutes.

head: Indicator
How it is measured
rows: Lead time
Opening to merge of human pull requests, as median and 90th percentile; bots are left out.
Release frequency
Stable releases per month; Elite is daily, High weekly, Medium monthly.
Revert rate
Merged pull requests whose title contains the word "Revert": a proxy of the change failure rate.
First review
Opening to the first review by someone other than the author.
Merge time by size
Median lead time per size, from changed lines: S under 50, M under 250, L under 1,000.

blocks.text: DORA measures delivery on internal deployments; public pull requests and releases only approximate it, so the bands are indications, not a verdict. When GitHub search does not index a repository, volumes come from the sample and some indicators are marked unavailable rather than shown as zero.

items: Instructions loaded on every request stay short and link to documents instead of copying them.
Wide searches and reviews run in subagents, so their output never fills the main context.
Cheaper models do mechanical work; the strongest model is kept for design and review.
Files are read by range, and hooks and quality gates do the checking, not extra turns.
Unrelated tasks start from a cleared context; long sessions are compacted with a focus.
One GraphQL request returns 100 branches with their last commit and divergence.
Protection comes from one filtered REST listing instead of one call per branch.
Results are cached for 10 minutes and shared between concurrent visitors.
The remaining quota is read from every response, and a reserve is never spent.
Each visitor has a daily allowance; repositories already analysed are free.

blocks.text: The records explain the context, the decision, the alternatives and the consequences of every structural choice: language and tooling, the AI workflow, releases, the command line, the dashboard, the public deployment, and the visitor allowance.
